intro: The coding rounds decide most of the result. These items cover the rest: the recruiter call, the resume deep-dives and Googleyness. Your notes stay on this computer.

items.title: Talk to your recruiter
items.why: Plan around the real process, not a guess.
prompts: How many rounds? Which are coding and which are Googleyness?
Is there an ML or domain round for this team?
Can the interview move 2 to 6 weeks later if you need more time?
Which languages can you use in the coding rounds?

items.title: Deep-dive story: your main LLM or agent project
items.why: Interviewers pick one resume line and dig for 10 minutes.
prompts: The problem and who used it.
Your design: models, tools, guardrails, and why.
How you measured quality: how the eval set was built, and how big it is.
One trade-off you made, and what you gave up.
What failed, and what you would change now.

items.title: Deep-dive story: knowledge graph or RAG work
items.why: A preferred skill in the job post. Expect follow-up questions.
prompts: Why a graph (or vectors) and not the other?
The schema or chunking you chose.
How you measured recall, and the number before and after.
Latency and cost per request.

items.title: Deep-dive story: a reliability problem you fixed
items.why: Shows distributed-systems sense without a design round.
prompts: What broke in production, and how you found out.
Retries that are safe to repeat (idempotency): how?
Failover between providers, and timeouts.
What you watch now so it does not happen again.

items.title: Defend every number on your resume
items.why: One number you cannot explain hurts more than no number.
prompts: For each metric: the baseline, how you measured it, and the sample size.
For any estimated number: how you estimated it.
What the number does NOT prove.
If you cannot explain it in 30 seconds, do not lead with it.

items.title: Honest answers about your timeline
items.why: Gaps and short jobs come up early. A calm one-line answer ends the topic.
prompts: Any gap: one sentence on what you did.
Short jobs: why you moved, said positively.
Practice history: say it plainly if old numbers do not match your current speed.

items.title: Responsible AI
items.why: Google asks this for any AI work that touches real people.
prompts: Where a human checks the model's decision.
What happens when the model is wrong, and how you know.
How sensitive data is stored and who can see it.
How you test for harmful or unsafe output.

items.title: Skills in the job post you have not used
items.why: Faking it fails at the first follow-up question.
prompts: List each one (for example a library, a query language, an algorithm family).
One honest line for each: what you know, and how you would start.
Spend one evening on the basics of the most likely one.

items.title: Explain your current system end to end
items.why: A 5-minute whiteboard of your own system shows real understanding.
prompts: Draw it: services, queues, databases, caches.
Why each part is there.
What breaks first at 10x traffic, and your fix.

items.title: Why Google, and why this team
items.why: Asked in almost every Googleyness round.
prompts: What the team builds, in one sentence.
How your experience fits it.
What you want to learn there.

items.title: Mock interviews with real people
items.why: Talking while coding is a separate skill. Only practice with people builds it.
prompts: From week 4: one coding mock a week with a person.
One behavioural mock using your STAR stories.
Log what went wrong as a mistake in the app after each one.
